issues.legal_issue: Mutation of property in revenue records does not transfer or extinguish ownership title.
material_facts: The property had been purchased in the name of the deceased owner and stood in her name in the revenue records.
After her death, her husband accepted a change of the revenue entry into the name of their son, and the entry was not challenged.
The husband had not relinquished or released his share, and the claim based on the mutation entry did not plead such a relinquishment.
issues.conclusion: The mutation entry did not divest the husband of his share; it was relevant to revenue collection and did not convey or extinguish title.
issues.legal_principle: A mutation entry neither creates nor extinguishes title and has no presumptive value on title; it enables collection of land revenue. The Court applied Balwant Singh v. Daulat Singh (1997) 7 SCC 137, which quoted and applied Sawarni v. Inder Kaur (1996) 6 SCC 223.

predicates.civil_title_dispute: A civil proceeding concerns competing claims to ownership of property.
predicates.revenue_mutation_recorded: A revenue authority entered a person’s name in property records after a proposed change of ownership.

issues.definition: When a civil title dispute includes a revenue mutation, the rule means that the mutation does not itself transfer or extinguish ownership title.

issues.legal_issue: On the death of a female owner, her surviving husband and son succeeded to the property in equal shares under the applicable statutory succession rules.
material_facts: The property had been purchased in the deceased woman's name.
When she died, she was survived by her husband and their son.
The lower appellate court held that the husband and son were each entitled to half of the property.
issues.conclusion: The husband and son succeeded as heirs to equal shares, and the lower appellate court’s decree recognizing those shares was restored.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Section 15 of the Hindu Succession Act, stating that the deceased owner’s husband and son succeeded to the property as heirs. It upheld the lower appellate court’s determination that each was entitled to half.

predicates.civil_property_succession_dispute: A civil proceeding concerns succession to property after its owner has died.
predicates.female_owner_died: A woman who owned the property died.
predicates.surviving_husband_and_son: The deceased woman was survived by her husband and her son.

issues.definition: When a civil property-succession dispute follows the death of a female owner survived by her husband and son, the rule means that they inherit equal shares.

issues.legal_issue: A request to use equitable powers to preserve a High Court decree does not prevent appellate interference when that decree rests on a serious legal error.
material_facts: The respondent asked the Court not to interfere with the High Court decree, relying on the parties’ circumstances and invoking Article 142 of the Constitution.
The High Court had treated the revenue mutation and the husband’s conduct as divesting him of his share, although he had not relinquished or released it.
The Court held that the High Court had misdirected itself and committed a serious error warranting interference.
issues.conclusion: The Court rejected the request not to interfere, set aside the High Court decree, and restored the lower appellate court’s decree.
issues.legal_principle: The respondent invoked Article 142 of the Constitution and cited Taherakhatoon (D) by Lrs. v. Salambin Mohammad (1999) 2 SCC 635 and Chandra Singh v. State of Rajasthan (2003) 6 SCC 545. The Court rejected the request in light of the serious error in the High Court’s decision; it did not state a broader test for exercising Article 142.

predicates.appeal_from_high_court_decree: A party brings an appeal challenging a High Court decree.
predicates.equitable_noninterference_requested: A party asks the appellate court to leave the challenged decree undisturbed on equitable grounds.
predicates.high_court_committed_serious_legal_error: The High Court’s decree rests on a serious legal error identified by the appellate court.

issues.definition: In an appeal from a High Court decree, when a party requests non-interference on equitable grounds but the decree rests on a serious legal error, the rule means that the appellate court may interfere with that decree.
